title: Macros
summary: Record a sequence of keys once and replay it on a hundred lines.

steps.title: Record, replay
body: qa        start recording into register a  (bottom line: "recording @a")
...       do the edit, ending where the NEXT edit should start (often with j or n)
50@a      replay it 50 times (stops early if a motion fails, e.g. at the end of the file)
A macro is just text in a register: `:reg a` shows it, and `"ap` pastes it so you can edit it and yank it back with `"ayy`... minus the newline (`0"ay$`).
The golden rule: **make the macro start and end in the same relative position**, so that it can be repeated. Begin with `0` or `^` to normalise the cursor, end with `j` to move to the next line.
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: Order the keystrokes that record a macro adding `;` at the end of a line and moving down, then run it on the next 9 lines.
steps.explain: Record (`qa`), append `;` (`A;` Esc), move to the next line (`j`), stop (`q`), replay nine times.

steps.prompt: The buffer is three lines `x`, `y`, `z` with the cursor on `x`. You record `qaI- <Esc>jq`, then press `@a`. What does the buffer contain?
steps.explain: Recording also performs the edit on `x`. `@a` replays it on `y`. `z` is untouched until you run it again.

steps.prompt: Match the keys to the effect.
pairs: run the macro in register a
run the macro once on every line

steps.prompt: Your macro works on the first line, but `20@a` leaves later lines half-edited. What is the most likely cause?
options: The macro does not start from a fixed position, such as `0` or `^`, so each run begins somewhere else
steps.explain: Normalise the starting position at the beginning of the macro and leave the cursor ready for the next run at the end.

steps.prompt: Recorded into the macro, or not?
items: an Esc you pressed while recording

steps.prompt: Run the macro in register `q` on every line from 5 to 20.
steps.explain: `:{range}norm {keys}` runs normal-mode keys on each line of the range.

steps.title: Real keys: record a macro
prompt: Record the edit for one line into register `a`, end it with `j` so it moves to the next line, stop recording, and replay it on the other three lines.
`qa` starts recording (Vim shows `recording @a`), `q` stops, `3@a` replays it three times, `@@` repeats the last macro.
steps.explain: A macro is only as good as its first line: use motions that work on every line (`I`, `A`, `0`, `$`, `f`), not counts of `l` that only fit the line you recorded on. Ending with `j` makes a count do the rest.

steps.title: A macro is just a register
prompt: A recorded macro is plain text in a register: `:reg a` shows it, and `:let @q = "..."` writes one directly. That is how you fix a macro, share it, or use it where you cannot press keys, as here.
Turn every line of `~/hosts.txt` into a quoted YAML list item (`web1.example.com` becomes `- "web1.example.com"`) with a macro in register `q`, run on every line with `:%norm @q`.
Inside the double quotes of `let`, `\<Esc>` is the Escape key and `\"` is a literal quote. Type it, then check the file.

checks.name: every host is a quoted YAML list item
checks.fail: `~/hosts.txt` is not right yet (`<` is the goal). Each line should be `- "host"`.

checks.name: no Vim is left running
checks.fail: A Vim process is still waiting for commands. Type `q!` and Enter in it, or `pkill vim`.

hints: The keys are: `I`, then `- "`, then Escape, then `A`, then `"`. In a `let` string Escape is `\<Esc>`.
`:%norm @q` runs the macro once on every line, starting at the beginning of each line.
steps.explain: `:%norm @q` (or `:g/pattern/norm @q`) beats `100@q`: it runs once per line, starts each run fresh at the line's start, and never runs past the end. In full-screen Vim, record with `qq ... q`, check it with `:reg q`, and paste it into your notes with `"qp`.
